reference.source: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Presents with anterior groin pain, often accompanied by mechanical symptoms such as clicking, catching, locking or a sensation of giving way.
The C-sign, in which the patient cups the hand over the lateral hip with thumb posterior and fingers into the groin, is a characteristic gesture localising deep intra-articular pain.
The anterosuperior labrum is the most frequently torn segment, reflecting the distribution of femoroacetabular contact stress.
The flexion-adduction-internal-rotation (FADIR) impingement test is the most sensitive provocation manoeuvre; a positive result reproduces the patient's groin pain.
Most symptomatic tears are secondary to an underlying driver: cam or pincer femoroacetabular impingement, acetabular dysplasia, capsular laxity or microinstability, or trauma.
Magnetic resonance arthrography is the imaging investigation of choice, and a diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection that abolishes pain confirms an intra-articular source.

Initial management is activity modification and physiotherapy targeting the deep hip stabilisers and lumbopelvic control; arthroscopic labral repair with correction of bony morphology is preferred to debridement where tissue quality allows.
Labral preservation restores the suction seal and fluid-film lubrication, so refixation generally outperforms simple excision in appropriately selected hips.
reference.pathophysiology: The acetabular labrum is a horseshoe-shaped fibrocartilaginous rim that deepens the socket, enlarges the articular contact area, and creates a suction seal that maintains intra-articular fluid pressurisation for cartilage nutrition and low-friction load transfer. Tears develop when the seal is repetitively overloaded: cam morphology drives abnormal femoral head-neck contact against the chondrolabral junction during flexion and internal rotation, pincer over-coverage crushes the labrum against the rim, acetabular dysplasia overloads the anterosuperior labrum as a secondary stabiliser, and capsular laxity or trauma imposes shear. Loss of the seal degrades fluid-film lubrication and cartilage nutrition, propagating chondral delamination and progression toward osteoarthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Femoroacetabular impingement without discrete labral tear
Early hip osteoarthritis with chondral wear
Iliopsoas tendinopathy or internal snapping hip
Athletic pubalgia (core muscle injury / sports hernia)
Lumbar spine referred pain or spinopelvic imbalance
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs including standing AP pelvis, Dunn lateral and false-profile views to assess cam/pincer morphology and dysplasia
Magnetic resonance arthrography of the hip
CT with three-dimensional reconstruction for detailed bony morphology and surgical planning
Assessment of femoral and acetabular version
Dynamic hip examination for impingement and instability
redFlags: Rest pain or night pain unrelieved by position, raising concern for neoplasm or infection
Fever or systemic upset suggesting septic arthritis
Inability to weight bear after minor trauma, suggesting occult femoral neck fracture
Rapidly progressive joint space narrowing indicating a closing window for joint preservation
reference.prognosis: Arthroscopic labral repair combined with correction of the underlying bony morphology gives good to excellent medium-term outcomes when performed before significant chondral damage. Established osteoarthritis with joint space narrowing predicts poorer results and a higher rate of conversion to arthroplasty.
pitfalls: Treating an incidentally imaged tear as the pain source, since asymptomatic labral tears are common on MRI, especially with increasing age.
Failing to address the causative cam or pincer morphology, which leads to recurrent tearing after isolated labral surgery.
Overlooking acetabular dysplasia and performing rim trimming that further destabilises an already under-covered hip.
Attributing all groin pain to the labrum while missing coexisting spinopelvic or lumbar contributions.
references: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: Initial conservative management with physiotherapy targeting hip and core mechanics, activity modification and simple analgesia
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection for symptomatic relief
Arthroscopic labral repair, or selective debridement, as definitive surgical treatment
Simultaneous correction of the underlying bony driver, with femoral osteochondroplasty for cam and rim trimming for pincer impingement
Periacetabular osteotomy where acetabular dysplasia is the underlying cause
Structured postoperative rehabilitation with graduated return to activity
Intervene before significant chondral damage, and consider arthroplasty where established osteoarthritis is present
